bodyHtml:
Movie dubbing: what it means and how it works

October 10, 2022
Communication | Audio Blog | Good to Know

A dubbed movie is a film in which the original dialogue has been replaced with a new recording in another language.

The actors you see on screen stay the same, but the voices you hear belong to voice actors who perform the translated script in time with the picture.

It is the reason a child in Manchester can watch an animated film from Japan or France and hear it in English.

This page explains what dubbing means, how film dubbing works step by step, how it compares with subtitling and voice-over, and what to consider if you want your own video dubbed.

What does dubbed mean in a movie?

Dubbing is the process of replacing the original speech in a film or programme with speech recorded in a different language.

The new dialogue is translated, adapted to fit the timing of the scene and, where possible, matched to the movement of the actors' lips.

You will also see the word used for fixing sound problems, such as re-recording dialogue that was unclear on set.

Dubbing is standard in animation, children's television, drama series and documentaries, and it is how many viewers in countries such as Germany, France, Spain and Italy meet foreign films.

Dubbing, subtitling and voice-over compared

These three methods all make video understandable in another language, but they work in different ways.

  • Dubbing replaces the original voices with new ones, usually synchronised to the actors' lips.
  • Subtitling keeps the original audio and adds translated text at the bottom of the screen.
  • Voice-over lays a translated narration over the original track, which stays faintly audible underneath. It is common in documentaries and corporate video.

Subtitling is usually the faster and more economical route, while dubbing gives viewers a more immersive experience because they can watch the screen without reading.

Many productions use both, so that viewers can choose.

How film dubbing works

Scripting and timing

Every dubbing project starts with a professional translator who turns the original script into the new language.

This is the trickiest stage, because jokes, sayings and cultural references rarely map word for word.

The result is a translation and an adaptation at the same time, since tone and emotion matter as much as meaning.

Timing is the biggest challenge.

A translated sentence must last about as long as the original, so the voice actor can say it naturally and still land on the visual cues in the scene.

Fitting words to visuals takes hours of careful work, even for a short scene.

Casting and recording

Next comes casting, which means finding voices that suit each character and the mood of the film.

Voice actors mirror the tone and inflection of the original performer, including the excitement, the singing and the sadness.

In the standard method, actors watch the original footage and read the script aloud in a studio.

A countdown of three beeps tells them when to start, and they speak on the fourth.

A second method, used mainly in France and Quebec, shows the lines on a strip of text that scrolls along the bottom of the screen while the film plays, so the actors read the dialogue in time with the picture.

Editing and mixing

Editing is the most painstaking stage, because the new dialogue has to sit inside the original soundtrack as if it had always been there.

Engineers first separate the original voices from the soundtrack to create a music and effects track, known as the M&E.

The new dialogue is then fitted into that track.

Audio post-production usually runs in three steps.

  1. Editing: choosing the best takes, combining them and trimming the music so it fits the picture without harming the sound.
  2. Mixing: balancing speech, music and sound effects, using tools such as equalisers, compressors and noise reduction.
  3. Mastering: levelling the finished audio so it sounds consistent on every device, from cinema speakers to phones and laptops.

Dubbing or subtitles: which do viewers prefer?

It is largely a matter of taste and habit.

Many viewers find subtitles tiring, because you have to follow the text and the picture at once.

Others feel that a dub changes the film, because the voices are no longer the original performers.

If you are learning a language, subtitled films with the original audio usually give you more to listen to than a dub.

For children, and for anyone who cannot read quickly, dubbing is often the easier choice.

Dubbing also widens a film's reach, since a release can go to cinemas and streaming services in many countries with every viewer hearing their own language.

Anime is a good example, as dubs helped bring Japanese animation to audiences who would not have watched it with subtitles.

Subtitling your video content

If your goal is to reach more viewers with a company video, advert or training film, subtitles are often the first step.

Subtitles keep your message readable when viewers watch without sound, for example in a busy office or on public transport.

They also make your content accessible.

The University of Manchester and RNID estimate that around 18 million people in the UK have some degree of hearing loss, and English subtitles or captions help many of them follow your video.

Professional subtitling follows technical rules on character limits per line, reading speed, spotting (the timing of each subtitle) and file formats.

Native-speaking audiovisual translators apply those rules and adapt your message so it feels natural to viewers in each market.

Dubbing your company video or film

Dubbing makes sense when you want viewers in a new market to experience your content as if it had been made for them.

You can choose lip-synced dubbing, as in a film or drama, or an unsynchronised voice-over, as in a documentary with an off-screen narrator.

Either way, the result depends on a good script, a well-cast voice and clean studio recording.

An amateur recording made on a basic microphone can undermine a video you have invested heavily in.

Share the languages, the running time and where the video will be shown, and you can request a quote for subtitles, voice-over or dubbing.

Frequently asked questions

What does it mean when a movie is dubbed?

It means the original spoken dialogue has been replaced by a recording in another language. Voice actors perform a translated script, timed to match the characters on screen.

What is the difference between dubbing and subtitles?

Dubbing replaces the audio, so you hear the film in your own language. Subtitles keep the original audio and show the translation as text at the bottom of the screen.

How is a film dubbed into another language?

A translator adapts the script to fit the timing of each scene, then voice actors record the lines while watching the footage. Sound engineers mix the new dialogue with the original music and effects track.

Is dubbing the same as voice-over?

No. Dubbing replaces the original voices and usually matches lip movement, while voice-over places a translated narration over the original audio. Voice-over is common in documentaries and corporate videos.

Can you dub or subtitle a company video for the UK market?

Yes. Professional audiovisual translators can subtitle or dub English video into other languages, or bring foreign-language video into English for UK audiences. The right method depends on your audience, your budget and where the video will be shown.
